# Statements

## Blocks and scope

Every block (`{ ... }`, loop body, branch) opens a scope. A name may shadow
an outer one in a nested block *(CLI only)*, but redeclaring a name in the
same scope is `` Duplicate declaration of `y` `` *(CLI only)*. A `let` in a
`for` initializer belongs to the loop (`tests/cases/cf_for`). A branch or
loop body that is a single statement rather than a block is accepted
*(CLI only)*.

<a id="let--const" style="scroll-margin-top: 65px"></a>

## `let` / `const`

- Every declaration needs an initializer (`` Variable `x` must be initialized ``
  *(CLI only)*) and takes its type from it; an annotation must match the
  initializer exactly (`Cannot initialize ... with ...`).
- Declaring a `void`-typed variable is `Cannot declare a variable of type void`
  *(CLI only)*. A local may be a destructuring pattern, `const { x, y } = p`
  or `let [a, b] = xs` ([Destructuring declarations](#destructuring-declarations));
  a module constant may not: `Destructured constants are not supported`
  (`reject_const_destructured`), because a module constant binds one name,
  and that name is the symbol the emitter writes. `var` is forbidden
  (`tests/cases/reject_var_keyword`, `reject_var_in_for`).
- `const` freezes the binding, not the contents: `xs[0] = 1` and
  `xs.push(1)` on a `const xs` are fine, `xs = []` is not
  (`tests/cases/arr_index_read_write`; `` Cannot assign to `x` because it is a const ``,
  `reject_assign_const`, `reject_cf_compound_const`).
- Locals live in an `alloca` slot; `opt -mem2reg` promotes them
  (`tests/cases/locals`).

## Destructuring declarations

A `const` or `let` in a function body, and the head of a `for...of`, may be an
object or an array pattern. Each name it binds is one read off the value on
the right, which is evaluated once and never copied:

```ts
const { x, y: py } = p        // x = p.x, py = p.y
let [a, , c] = xs             // a = xs[0], c = xs[2]
for (const { x, y } of points) { ... }
```

- **An object pattern** reads a class or interface value. Each entry is a
  field's name, `x`, or a field renamed, `y: py`; the name's type is the
  field's. A missing field is `` Cannot destructure field `z`: Point has no
  such field `` (NL2776, `reject_destructure_field`).
- **An array pattern** reads an array. Each name is one element read by its
  position, with the bounds check of `xs[i]`; a hole, `[a, , c]`, skips a
  position. An element past the end panics, `index out of range: 5 >= 3`
  (`destructure_out_of_range`), where TypeScript would bind `undefined`: a
  name in Nish always holds a value of its type.
- **A `for...of` head** destructures each element of an array
  (`destructure_for_of`). Over a `Set` or an iterator it is NL2783
  (`reject_destructure_for_of_set`). Over a `Map` it is NL2375, the
  refusal any `for...of` over a `Map` gets, before the pattern is read: a
  `Map`'s entries are `[key, value]` pairs of two types, a tuple, which this
  version does not have (`reject_destructure_for_of_map`,
  `reject_map_iter_entries`).
- A name is a fresh local: `let` names may be assigned, `const` names may
  not. A struct's fields are read through its pointer, so
  `const { x } = p` on a stack-allocated `p` costs one load
  (`destructure_stack`).

Refused, each with its own diagnostic and test:

| Pattern | Diagnostic | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[a, b] = xs`, `({ x } = p)`, `({ x: px } = p)` (assignment) | NL2771 `Destructuring assignment is not supported` | `reject_destructure_assignment`, `reject_destructure_assignment_object` |
| `{ x = 0 }`, `[a = 1]` (a default) | NL2772 | `reject_destructure_default` |
| `[a, ...rest]`, `{ x, ...others }` | NL2773 | `reject_destructure_rest` |
| `{ p: { x } }`, `[[a]]` (nested) | NL2774 | `reject_destructure_nested` |
| `{ ["x"]: a }`, `{ "x": a }` | NL2775 | `reject_destructure_key` |
| a value that may be absent, `Point \| null` or a `V \| undefined` from `Map.get` | NL2777, narrow it first | `reject_destructure_nullable`, `reject_destructure_undefined` |
| a `Map` | NL2778, read each value with `get` | `reject_destructure_map` |
| a `string` | NL2779, read each character by its index | `reject_destructure_string` |
| an object pattern over a number | NL2780 | `reject_destructure_object_of_number` |
| an array pattern over an object | NL2781 | `reject_destructure_array_of_object` |
| `let { x }: Point;` (no initializer) | NL2782 | `reject_destructure_uninitialized` |
| a parameter, `({ x }: Point) => x` | `Destructured parameters are not supported` | `reject_param_destructured` |
| a module constant | `Destructured constants are not supported` | `reject_const_destructured` |

A pattern over `await` is refused with `Destructuring is not supported`
(`nl2193_destructuring_local`), but for the answers of
`const [a, b] = await awaitAll(f(x), g(y))`
([Async functions](declarations.md#async-functions-async-and-await)).

## Expression statements

Any expression may be a statement; its value is discarded *(CLI only)*.
`console.log(...)`, `process.exit(...)`, `writeFileSync(...)` and
`appendFileSync(...)` return `void` and may appear *only* as statements
(`can only be used as a statement`, `tests/cases/reject_console_log_as_value`).

## `return`

The expression's type must equal the declared return type
(`Return type mismatch: function returns ... but expression is ...`); a bare
`return` is valid only in a `void` function
(`Expected a return value of type ...`) (`tests/cases/entry_main_void`).

<a id="if--else" style="scroll-margin-top: 65px"></a>

## `if` / `else`

The condition must be `boolean`: there is no truthiness
(`Condition must be boolean, got i32 (Nish has no truthiness)`,
`tests/cases/reject_cf_nonbool_cond`). `else if` chains are nested `if`s
(`tests/cases/cf_if`, `cf_if_else_chain`).

<a id="while-do--while-for" style="scroll-margin-top: 65px"></a>

## `while`, `do ... while`, `for`

- Conditions must be `boolean` (`tests/cases/cf_while`, `cf_do_while`,
  `cf_for`).
- `for (init; cond; update)`: every clause is optional; the initializer is
  a `let`/`const` list or an expression (`tests/cases/cf_break_continue`
  for `for (;;)`; expression initializer *(CLI only)*).
- Loop variables are ordinary mutable locals; there is no restriction on
  assigning them (`tests/cases/cf_collatz`).
- A loop whose condition is absent or the literal `true` and whose body has
  no `break` for it never falls through (see Termination); every other loop
  may run zero times (`tests/cases/cf_while`, `firstPowerOver`).

## `for (const x of a)`

- `a` must be an array (`` `for...of` requires an array, got string ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_arr_forof_non_array`), or a walk of the global `Map` or
  `Set`: `m.keys()`, `m.values()`, a `Set` itself, `s.keys()` or `s.values()`
  ([`Map` and `Set`](builtins.md#map-and-set)), or a `Channel` from `nish/threads`, which
  takes values off it ([Channels](declarations.md#channels-channelt)); `x` gets the element type and
  must not be annotated
  (`` The `for...of` variable takes the element type; remove the annotation ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_arr_forof_annotation`) or initialised
  (`` The `for...of` variable cannot have an initializer ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_arr_forof_initializer`); exactly one variable
  (`` `for...of` declares exactly one variable ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_arr_forof_two_vars`); the head is a declaration rather
  than an assignment to something already declared
  (`` `for...of` needs a `const` or `let` declaration ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_arr_forof_expression`); `let x` makes
  it assignable, `const x` does not (`tests/cases/reject_arr_forof_const_assign`).
  `for await` is not supported (`` `for await` is not supported here ``,
  `tests/wordings/nl2133_for_await`), and `for...in` is forbidden
  ([Rejected statements](#rejected-statements)).
- `a` is evaluated once; `a.length` is re-read every iteration, so a `push`
  inside the body extends the iteration, as JavaScript's array iterator does
  (`tests/cases/arr_for_of`). `break` and `continue` work
  (`tests/cases/arr_for_of`).

## `switch`

```typescript
switch (node.kind) {
  case KIND_IF:
  case KIND_WHILE:
    return checkBranch(node);
  case KIND_CALL:
    return checkCall(node);
  default:
    return ERROR;
}
```

- The discriminant is an **integer** (`i32`, `i64`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`;
  so a `number` in the default mode but not under `--number-mode f64`) or a
  numeric **`enum`** ([Enums](declarations.md#enums)), which is an `i32` in the jump table.
  Any other type is `` `switch` requires an integer discriminant, got <type> ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_switch_string`). Only an integer switch lowers to
  LLVM's `switch` and a jump table; a string switch would have been a chain
  of `nish_str_eq` calls wearing a switch's clothes, and `if`/`else` says that
  honestly.
- Every `case` label is an **integer constant expression** of the
  discriminant's type: a literal, its negation, a module constant, or an enum
  member
  (`` `case` label must be an integer literal, a module constant, or an enum member ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_switch_case_not_constant`; `` `case` label is i64 but
  the discriminant is i32 ``, `reject_switch_case_type`). A literal takes the
  discriminant's width, so `case 1:` on an `i64` switch is an `i64` one — and
  on an enum switch it is `` `case` label is i32 but the discriminant is Kind ``
  (`reject_enum_case_label`), because the integer a member stands for is not
  the member.
- Labels are distinct (``Duplicate `case` label `1` in this `switch` ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_switch_duplicate_case`), and there is at most one
  `default` (`` `switch` has more than one `default` clause `` *(CLI only)*),
  which may appear anywhere among the clauses.
- **A clause falls through, as in TypeScript.** A clause whose statements do
  not end in `break`, `return`, `continue` or `process.exit` runs on into the
  next clause's statements; the IR branches into the next clause's block, with
  no flag (`tests/cases/cf_switch_fallthrough`, `cf_label_walks`). An **empty**
  clause falls through the same way, which is how `case 1: case 2:` gives
  several labels one body (`tests/cases/cf_switch`). A clause reached by
  falling into it is reached with either label's value: a tag test does not
  narrow there (`reject_switch_fall_narrow`), and a local the clauses above it
  assigned holds its declared type.
- A clause cannot declare a variable directly; wrap its body in a block
  (``A `case` clause cannot declare a variable directly ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_switch_case_declaration`). Clauses share one scope in
  TypeScript, so a declaration in one would be visible but unassigned in the
  ones below it.
- `break` inside a `switch` leaves the switch, not an enclosing loop;
  `continue` looks past the switch to the loop
  (`tests/cases/cf_switch_break`). A labelled `break` or `continue` names
  the loop instead (see below, `cf_label_switch`).
- A `switch` terminates (see Termination) when no `break` targets it, its
  last clause terminates, and it has a `default` or is a complete `switch` on a
  union's tag, whose labels name every variant
  ([Discriminated unions](types.md#discriminated-unions), `tests/cases/union_switch`).
  A `switch` on an integer or a plain enum without a `default` never
  terminates, whatever its labels (`reject_union_switch_enum`).

<a id="break--continue" style="scroll-margin-top: 65px"></a>

## `break` / `continue`

A label goes on a loop, a block or a `switch` (`outer: for (...)`,
`check: { ... }`, `sw: switch (...)`); on any other statement it is refused
(`` Labeled statements are forbidden in Nish except on a loop, a block or a
`switch` ``, `tests/cases/reject_label_if`). `break label` leaves the statement
the label names, from any depth inside it; `continue label` starts the next turn
of the loop it names. Each lowers to the branch a hand-kept `done` flag would
take — to that statement's exit block or its loop's step block — with no flag
(`tests/cases/cf_label_loops`, `cf_label_block`, `cf_label_switch`,
`cf_label_walks`). Leaving a scoped pass or a `Map` walk this way releases it
as an unlabelled exit would, and a `Secret` local a labelled exit skips past
must be wiped first (`reject_label_secret_break`, `reject_label_secret_block`).

- A label is not reused inside the statement it names (``Duplicate label
  'outer'``, `reject_label_duplicate`).
- `continue label` names a loop (`` A `continue` can only jump to a label of
  an enclosing loop ``, `reject_label_continue_block`), and `break label` a
  statement around it (`` A `break` can only jump to a label of an enclosing
  statement ``, `reject_label_unknown`).
- A jump does not leave an arrow for a label outside it (``Jump target cannot
  cross function boundary``, `reject_label_crosses_arrow`).

Unlabelled, `break` needs an
enclosing loop or `switch` (`` `break` outside of a loop or `switch` ``,
`tests/cases/reject_cf_break_outside`) and `continue` an enclosing loop
(`` `continue` outside of a loop ``, `reject_cf_continue_outside`), which it
finds past any `switch` in between. `tests/cases/cf_break_continue`,
`cf_switch_break`.

## `throw` (removed)

`throw` is forbidden by Phase 0 (`tests/cases/reject_throw`). Until WP16 it
compiled to `llvm.trap` — it aborted the process and discarded its value —
which made it an abort wearing the syntax of error handling, and let a program
report a failure in a way no caller could see. The two things it was used for
have their own spelling now:

- a failure a caller should handle is a **[`Result<T, E>`](result-and-error-handling.md)**;
- an invariant that cannot hold is **`panic(message)`**, which keeps the
  message `throw` threw away.

`try`/`catch`/`finally` is forbidden for the same reason
(`tests/cases/reject_try_catch`).

<a id="processexitcode-as-a-statement" style="scroll-margin-top: 65px"></a>

## `process.exit(code)` as a statement

Terminates the process with `code` (an `i32`) and, for control-flow
purposes, the current path: a non-`void` function may end with it
(`tests/cases/process_exit`), and code after it is
`Unreachable code after process.exit` (`tests/cases/reject_exit_unreachable`).

## Termination, definite return, and unreachable code

A statement *terminates* when control cannot fall out of it: `return`,
`break`, `continue`, `process.exit(...)`, `panic(...)`; an `if` whose branches
both terminate; a `switch` with a `default` or one complete on a union's tag,
no `break` aimed at it and a terminating last clause; a loop with no condition or the condition `true` and
no `break` aimed at it; a labelled block whose statements terminate and no
`break` names. A `break` aimed at a statement is an unlabelled one directly
inside it or a labelled one that names it from any depth, so a `break outer`
in an inner loop makes `outer: while (true)` one that may finish. Any other
loop may run zero times and does not terminate. Rules (`src/statements.ts`, `checker.ts`):

- A non-`void` function's body must terminate
  (`must return a value of type i32 on every path`,
  `tests/cases/reject_missing_return`, `reject_cf_missing_return_loop`;
  `if (true) { return 1; }` alone is not enough *(CLI only)*).
- A statement after a terminating one is `Unreachable code after <what>`,
  where `<what>` is `return`, `break`, `continue`, `process.exit`,
  `` an `if` whose branches all return ``, `` a `switch` whose clauses all
  return ``, or `an infinite loop`
  (`tests/cases/reject_unreachable`, `reject_cf_unreachable_after_break`,
  `reject_exit_unreachable`; the `if` form *(CLI only)*).

## Mistakes every type accepts

Some lines type-check and still cannot be what their author meant. Rust
warns about most of them and Clippy denies the rest. Here each one is an
error, because it is a bug far more often than it is a choice. Each rule fires only
where the answer is certain, and each has a spelling that says "on purpose".
Rules (`src/hygiene.ts`):

- **A local is read at least once** (NL2712). A `let` or `const`, a
  `for...of` binding included, that nothing reads is
  `` `x` is declared but never read `` (`reject_unread_local`,
  `reject_unread_for_of`). Storing into a local is not reading it: `n++` or
  `n += 1` on a line of its own, or as a `for` loop's step, writes `n` and
  uses nothing, so a counter nothing reports is
  `` `n` is assigned but its value is never read ``
  (`reject_unread_local_written`); `const m = n++` reads it. A capture by an
  arrow is a read. A lone name on its own line, `x;`, is not a read
  (`reject_unread_lone_name`). A name that starts with `_` is never reported,
  which is how a loop that only counts its turns is written:
  `for (const _item of xs)` (`hygiene_quiet`). A `using` binding is exempt,
  because its block's end uses it. A `Result` local has its own rule (NL2032,
  [Result and error handling](result-and-error-handling.md)).
- **A statement has an effect** (NL2713). An expression statement with no
  call, `new`, store, `++`, `--` or `await` anywhere in it is
  `This statement has no effect` (`reject_no_effect_statement`,
  `reject_no_effect_member`). `state === next;` adds
  `` (to assign, write `=`) ``. A lone name is left to the rule above.
- **A value is not assigned to itself** (NL2714). `x = x`, `p.x = p.x`
  and `xs[i] = xs[i]` do nothing (`reject_self_assign`).
- **An operator has two different operands** (NL2715). With the same
  operand on both sides, `===` `!==` `==` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=` `&&` `||` `&`
  `|` `^` `-` `/` `%` give an answer that does not depend on it, so the
  expression is refused (`reject_same_operands`, `reject_same_operands_index`).
  Two operands are the same when they are the same pure expression over the
  same variables: the same local, field path, element by the same index, or
  the same operators over those. A literal-only expression is not refused. On
  `f32` and `f64`, `x !== x` is the NaN test and `x - x === 0` the finite
  test, so only `<` and `>` are refused there, which are false for every
  value (`reject_same_operands_float_ordered`). To compare a value with
  itself on purpose, copy it to a second `const` first (`hygiene_quiet`).
- **An `else if` tests something new** (NL2716). A condition the same as an
  earlier one in the same `if`/`else if` chain can never pass, because the
  earlier branch took every case it would match (`reject_repeated_condition`).
  A condition with a call in it can answer differently the second time, and
  is not compared.
- **An unsigned value is not compared with zero for its sign** (NL2717).
  `u < 0` and `0 > u` are always false, and `u >= 0` and `0 <= u` always
  true, for a `u8`, `u16`, `u32` or `u64` (`reject_unsigned_zero`,
  `reject_unsigned_zero_reversed`).

These findings are reported only once every other rule has passed: a program
with any other error is told that error alone (`reject_hygiene_held`), so
an unread local never crowds out the error that left it unread. They are held
to the program's own package and the standard library. A dependency's
findings are left to its author, as Cargo caps the lints of a crate it pulls
in.

## Rejected statements

`with` (`tests/cases/reject_with_statement`), `try` (`reject_try_catch`),
`debugger` (`reject_debugger`), a label on a statement other than a loop, a
block or a `switch` (`reject_label_if`),
`var` (`reject_var_keyword`), `for...in` (`` `for...in` is forbidden in Nish
(it enumerates property names, and object layout is fixed at compile time); use
`for...of` ``, NL1056, `reject_for_in`), nested `function`, `enum`, `type`,
`namespace` (`reject_namespace`), `declare global` (`reject_declare_global`).
`with`, `try` and `var` are not reserved: a function or a variable may be
called one, and a statement opens only where the word could not be that
name. `with (…)` is the statement when a statement follows it on the same
line, and `var` when a name follows it on the same line. `try` is the
statement when a block follows it on the same line, or when a block follows
it and a handler follows that block (`catch {`, `catch (e) {` or `finally {`,
not a call such as `finally();`), whatever line breaks and comments sit
between (`reject_try_allman_catch`, `reject_try_allman_finally`,
`reject_try_comment_newline`). A catch binding may be a name or a
destructuring pattern, with or without an annotation, and is refused the same
way (`reject_try_catch_destructured`). So a `try`-named block followed by
`catch(<a binding>)` — a name or a pattern, `catch(n)` or `catch([n])` — and
then a block is a `try` statement, even where 0.13.0 read a call to a function
named `catch` (`reject_try_catch_call_newline`,
`reject_try_catch_pattern_call_newline`): the one shape of program this rule
stopped compiling. An argument that is no binding, such as `catch([1, 2])` or
`catch({ first: 1 })`, is the call it was (`tests/parser/names-catch-array.ts`,
`names-catch-object.ts`). A line break inside a block comment counts as
one, as it does for semicolon insertion. So `try` alone on a line before a
block that nothing handles is a name and a block, as it was before
(`tests/parser/names.ts`). `tsc` reserves all three, so this is Nish
accepting what TypeScript does not, as it did before these statements
parsed.
`enum` and `type` are top-level declarations ([Enums](declarations.md#enums),
[Type aliases](declarations.md#type-aliases)); it is only inside a function body that they are
a rejected statement.

The empty statement, a lone `;` where a statement stands, is refused in a
body: `Unsupported statement in Phase 1: EmptyStatement` (NL2260,
`tests/cases/reject_stmt_empty`). It is the sentence every statement kind with
no checker gets, named by its syntax kind as a nested `function` or `import`
is; every other such kind is refused earlier by a rule of its own. It is
refused where a body is checked, so a `;` in a template nothing instantiates
still compiles, as it did in every release. A `;` at the top level is the
syntax error `` a module holds only `function`, `class`, `interface`, `const`,
`type`, `enum` and `import`, found `;` `` (NL0001).
